ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. Experiments revealed preferential adsorption of branched alkanes over their linear isomers on specific zeolites with tubular pore systems such as SAPO-5 and Mordenite. $ ^{24-28} $ Molecular simulations indicated that in such zeolites, depending on conditions, branched alkanes are preferentially adsorbed at the expense of linear isomers. $ ^{29-34} $ The present manuscript discusses the mechanisms of shape selectivity in n- and isoalkane adsorption on zeolite MCM-22. This zeolite with IZA code MWW is a relatively new synthetic material that has an unusual and quite complex pore structure. $ ^{35} $ Its framework is composed of two independent pore systems. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. The Gibbs free energies of the zeolite support consist of only vibrational and electronic contributions. The expressions of all enthalpy and entropy contributions can be found in Ref. [38].

The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

In the following appendix , we derive the entropy of adsorption in the case of infinite dilution and show how it may be related to familiar thermodynamic quantities ( cf . eq 5 ) . To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via

$$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$

$$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$

where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as

$$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$

where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows.

descriptor_candidates.name: occ_vol_confinement_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: The entropy loss fraction (s_gas - s_ads)/R correlates with a confinement descriptor combining framework-to-pore diameter ratio and accessible volume density: tighter, less voluminous frameworks cause larger entropy loss. Adding a nonlinear re-expression of Vol, AV, lsd_p, lsd_f reduces MAE of entropy loss/R relative to using the 14 raw inputs alone.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E01, E02) shows confinement extent controls entropy loss and that occupiable volume alone predicts it linearly. Inference: the ratio of pore-limiting to largest diameter (lsd_p/lsd_f) proxies the degree of rotational/translational restriction within the pore; nonlinear combination captures curvature in this relation. E10 supports that molecules compressed into pores smaller than free molecular size lose more configurational freedom.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If, on held-out zeolite/adsorbate pairs, this descriptor's neural network model does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below the 14-input baseline, or if lsd_p/lsd_f shows no monotonic relation to entropy loss within framework families, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: shape_anisotropy_mismatch
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss is maximized when adsorbate size anisotropy (SPAN) mismatches the pore-limiting diameter (lsd_p) and when the molecular gyration/diameter shape (GeDi vs PBF) deviates from circularity, because rotational degrees of freedom are quenched asymmetrically in tubular pores.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E01) notes molecular shape and confinement interaction determines ΔS_conf; E04 shows shape-selective steric matching alters adsorption states; E07 shows molecular symmetry affects confined diffusion (a proxy for rotational freedom). Inference: combining molecular elongation (SPAN/lsd_p) with shape asymmetry (GeDi/PBF deviation) should nonlinearly predict rotational entropy loss beyond what either does alone.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the residual entropy loss after the baseline model shows no significant correlation with SPAN/lsd_p or GeDi/PBF deviation (e.g., permutation test p > 0.05 on residuals), or if including this descriptor does not lower MAE, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: rotational_free_space_density
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss fraction scales with a 'rotational free space density': molecules in frameworks with large pore-to-free-sphere diameter differences (lsd_f - lsd_p), low accessible surface-to-volume ratios (LabuteASA/Vol), and low product of framework density and accessible volume retain less entropy, because accessible pockets become cage-like (rotational arrest) rather than channel-like.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E01, E02) distinguishes framework-dependent entropy loss (TON > FAU) and ties it to accessible volume; E05 notes rotational degrees of freedom are reduced (by ~1.28) upon confinement; E09 derives entropy loss from the configurational partition function affected by accessible configuration space. Inference: the geometry difference lsd_f - lsd_p discriminates cage vs channel topologies, modulating how much configuration space is removed per unit volume.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this descriptor to the 14-input neural network fails to decrease MAE of entropy loss/R on held-out data, or if the sign of the lsd_f - lsd_p effect on entropy loss is opposite to prediction (larger free-sphere minus pore diameter should increase loss), the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: surface_contact_cage_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss fraction (s_gas - s_ads)/R increases with a contact-to-cage index: molecules confined in frameworks where the accessible surface-to-volume contact density (LabuteASA/Vol) is high relative to framework density, and where the free-sphere to pore diameter ratio is large (lsd_f/lsd_p squared), lose more entropy because adsorbate-framework wall contact fraction rises, quenching translational and rotational degrees of freedom. Adding this descriptor to the 14-input neural network reduces MAE of entropy loss/R below the current best 0.5607.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from source evidence: E01 shows framework-dependent entropy loss (TON largest, FAU smallest) tied to confinement geometry; E02 shows occupiable volume alone predicts entropy loss, implying surface-to-volume geometry matters; E05 reports rotational entropy reduced more than translational (1.28 vs 1) upon confinement, suggesting wall proximity specifically suppresses rotation. The square of lsd_f/lsd_p encodes nonlinear intensification of restriction as pore diameter approaches free molecular size (E10). Unlike the retained descriptor (volume density × diameter ratio), this one uses surface contact density and a squared diameter ratio, probing a different mechanism: wall-contact frequency rather than volumetric crowding.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this descriptor does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5607 on the same evaluation, or if the squared diameter ratio term shows no monotonic relation to residuals of the baseline model (permutation test p > 0.05), the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: moment_asymmetry_aperture_mismatch
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss fraction is largest for molecules with high principal-moment anisotropy (PMI3/PMI1) confined in pores whose volume, normalized by the product of pore-limiting diameter and molecular span, is small: anisotropic molecules in tight pores lose rotational entropy disproportionately because only one rotational axis retains freedom. Adding this descriptor reduces MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the 14-input baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E07 shows molecular symmetry affects confined rotational/translational dynamics (different rotational free-energy landscapes for symmetric vs asymmetric molecules in AFI); E01 states the role of molecular shape and confinement interaction in ΔS_conf remains undetermined, implying shape-dependent terms are unexplored; E04 shows shape-matching between adsorbate and pore creates distinct adsorption states. Inference: PMI ratio is a more principled rotational-anisotropy proxy than the previously tested SPAN/lsd_p ratio (which failed, marginal improvement -0.026); combining PMI anisotropy with a volume-based confinement tightness term captures a mechanism distinct from the failed shape_anisotropy_mismatch, which used span mismatch instead of moment anisotropy and lacked a free-space term.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the residual entropy loss after the baseline plus retained descriptor shows no correlation with PMI3/PMI1 (permutation p > 0.05), or if including this descriptor fails to improve MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5607, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: accessibility_deficit_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss fraction scales with an accessibility deficit: when the geometric frame volume (Vol) exceeds the accessible volume estimated from AV and density, and when the surface-area-to-pore-volume ratio (ASA/AV) is high, molecules occupy configurations near walls in cage-like pockets with restricted configurational space, so a larger fraction of gas-phase entropy is lost. Adding this descriptor reduces MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5607.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence: E02 identifies occupiable volume as the single predictive material descriptor, implying the contrast between total and accessible volume encodes confinement beyond either alone; E09 derives entropy loss from the configurational partition function, i.e., the accessible configuration space volume; E01 shows cage-like frameworks (FAU, small loss) versus channel-like frameworks (TON, large loss) differ in entropy loss at similar chemistry. Inference: the ASA/AV ratio discriminates cage topologies (large surface per pore volume, many wall contacts) from open channels, and the volume-accessibility deficit term is dimensionally normalized by lsd_f. This probes framework topology via surface-to-pore-volume ratio, a mechanism not tested in any prior candidate.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this descriptor fails to reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5607 on held-out data, or if the sign of the ASA/AV effect on residual entropy loss is opposite to prediction (higher surface-to-pore-volume should increase loss), the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss fraction (s_gas - s_ads)/R increases when the intermediate-to-minimum principal moment ratio (PMI2/PMI1, a measure of how 'locked' the lowest-energy rotational mode is) is large AND the free space around the molecule per unit molecular volume, (lsd_f - lsd_p)*SPAN/Vol, is small: molecules with one nearly fixed rotation axis confined in near-constricting pores lose rotational entropy beyond what volumetric descriptors capture. Adding this descriptor to the 14-input network lowers MAE of entropy loss/R below the current best 0.5528.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E07) shows molecular symmetry qualitatively changes confined rotational free-energy landscapes in AFI; (E05) quantifies that rotational entropy is reduced more than translational entropy (factor 1.28 vs 1) upon confinement; (E01) states the shape-confinement role in Delta S_conf remains undetermined. Inference: the intermediate principal moment ratio distinguishes prolate/oblate rotational restriction that PMI3/PMI1 (tested and failed in round 2) does not, and the free-space-per-volume term (lsd_f - lsd_p scaled by SPAN over Vol) is a new geometric normalization distinct from all previously scored candidates. This is an inferred mechanism, not an established literature relation.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this descriptor does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5528 under the same evaluation protocol, or if the residual entropy loss of the baseline+retained model shows no monotonic trend with PMI2/PMI1 within molecule families (permutation test p > 0.05), the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: packing_saturation_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss fraction peaks with a packing saturation index: frameworks whose accessible volume fraction (density*AV on the source numerical scale) is high but whose pore-limiting diameter is much smaller than the free-sphere diameter (lsd_p/lsd_f to the 8th power, encoding a steep nonlinear penalty near the constriction threshold of ~80% of free molecular size) force molecules into constricted, vibration-like adsorption states; the ASA/LabuteASA ratio re-weights by accessible-vs-molecular surface scale. Adding this descriptor reduces MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5528.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E10) reports molecules can penetrate pores only down to ~80% of their free molecular size via framework distortion, implying a sharp threshold behavior in pore-to-molecule size ratio; (E02) identifies occupiable volume as the single predictive material descriptor; (E01) shows entropy loss differs strongly across frameworks (TON > FAU). Inference: a high-power (exponent 8, constant within allowed range) rational term captures the threshold-like loss of configurational freedom as lsd_p approaches lsd_f, while the accessible volume fraction controls how many such constricted sites exist per gram. This threshold mechanism differs from the linear diameter ratios used in all prior candidates.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If including this descriptor fails to reduce MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5528, or if the high-power diameter-ratio term contributes no monotonic effect on baseline residuals (permutation test p > 0.05), the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: entropy_free_space_residual
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss fraction is governed by a normalized free-volume-per-pore-count term divided by framework density, Vol/lsd_p^3/density (number of pore-sized cages per unit framework mass, on the source density scale), modulated by an exponential matching factor exp(-|PBF - lsd_p|/(PBF+lsd_p)) between the molecule's parallel projection extent (PBF) and the pore-limiting diameter: entropy loss is largest when many small cages coexist with near-perfect size matching (matching factor near 1), because adsorbates are then locked in single-configuration cage sites. Adding this descriptor reduces MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5528.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Source evidence (E09) derives adsorption entropy from the configurational partition function, i.e., the accessible configuration-space volume; (E02) shows occupiable volume alone predicts entropy loss linearly, implying cage counting (Vol normalized by pore volume and mass) encodes the number of distinct sites; (E04) shows close size matching produces substantially different, shape-selective adsorption states; (E01) shows cage-like FAU loses less entropy than channel-like TON. Inference: the cage-count term is a new re-expression of Vol, lsd_p, and density never used in prior rounds (previous candidates used volume ratios or diameter ratios alone), and the PBF-to-lsd_p matching factor probes the size-match mechanism with a molecular geometry input (PBF) not yet combined with pore diameters.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this descriptor does not lower MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5528, or if |PBF - lsd_p| shows no correlation with residual entropy loss after the baseline+retained descriptors (permutation test p > 0.05), or if the cage-count term has the opposite sign to prediction, the hypothesis is falsified.

retained.name: occ_vol_confinement_ratio
retained.hypothesis: The entropy loss fraction (s_gas - s_ads)/R correlates with a confinement descriptor combining framework-to-pore diameter ratio and accessible volume density: tighter, less voluminous frameworks cause larger entropy loss. Adding a nonlinear re-expression of Vol, AV, lsd_p, lsd_f reduces MAE of entropy loss/R relative to using the 14 raw inputs alone.

retained.name: surface_contact_cage_index
retained.hypothesis: Entropy loss fraction (s_gas - s_ads)/R increases with a contact-to-cage index: molecules confined in frameworks where the accessible surface-to-volume contact density (LabuteASA/Vol) is high relative to framework density, and where the free-sphere to pore diameter ratio is large (lsd_f/lsd_p squared), lose more entropy because adsorbate-framework wall contact fraction rises, quenching translational and rotational degrees of freedom. Adding this descriptor to the 14-input neural network reduces MAE of entropy loss/R below the current best 0.5607.
